extracted.intended_audience: NLP / multimodal affective computing researchers working on sarcasm and humor classification in code-mixed conversational data
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating models to classify utterances as sarcastic and/or humorous in Hindi-English code-mixed conversational dialogs using textual, acoustic, and (optionally) visual modalities with attention-based fusion mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precision, recall, F1-score, and accuracy to evaluate sarcasm detection and humor classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report class-wise precision/recall/F1 and overall accuracy; provide confusion matrices and per-dialog example analyses to explain errors and trade-offs (e.g., precision/recall values shown for sample dialog and aggregated sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal feature usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage textual, acoustic, and visual modalities for utterance classification; evaluate uni-modal, bi-modal, and tri-modal variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare models trained on each modality separately and in combination; note that visual features may be ineffective if video frames are low quality (paper: 'results using only visual features are far from satisfactory' due to low quality frames).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic feature role and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acoustic features mainly capture intensity, excitation mode, pitch, etc., and lack semantic entities; alone they yield low F1 despite reasonable accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acoustic-only models (LSTM(A)) achieved accuracies of 73.8% and 52.3% but F1-scores of only 21.6% and 21.5%; combine acoustics with textual features intelligently (filtering/gating) to exploit complementary signals rather than treating them as noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual utterance embedding: hierarchical attention vs mean vector
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchical utterance-level attention (H-ATNU) extracts richer textual features than a mean of constituent word embeddings (Tavg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models using hierarchical attention produce substantially higher F1 (examples: 68.8% and 71.7% vs 56.3% and 67.8% for sarcasm and humor respectively); prefer attention-based textual embeddings for stronger semantic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utterance-level hierarchical attention for acoustic (H-ATNA) vs raw acoustic (A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying utterance-level hierarchical attention over acoustic modality (H-ATNA) decreased performance relative to using raw acoustic features (A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors observed a performance decrease of ~7 and ~10 F1 points for sarcasm and humor respectively when using H-ATNA instead of A; therefore, prefer raw acoustic representation (A) in this setup unless further tuning justifies attention over acoustics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialog-level contextual attention (C-ATND)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dialog-level modality-specific contextual attention mechanism learns relevant context to capture below-the-surface semantics for the target utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating C-ATND improved F1 (e.g., ∼8 and ∼26 point improvements in F1 for sarcasm and humor when added to LSTM(A)); it reduces false negatives by attending to underrepresented sarcastic/humorous classes. Use it to exploit nearby contextual utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context attention width selection (AtnWidthD and AtnWidthU)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of contextual utterances considered in attention computation affects performance: AtnWidthU (utterance-level) in [2,5] with optimal AtnWidthU=3; AtnWidthD (dialog-level) optimal = 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing AtnWidthD beyond five degrades performance because sarcasm/humor context typically resides in close proximity; smaller widths may not provide sufficient context. Choose AtnWidthD=5 and AtnWidthU=3 as starting points and validate on dev set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bi-modal/tri-modal fusion and gating/filtering mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine modality-specific LSTMs and fuse representations using dialog-level contextual attention modules and a gating/filtering mechanism to extract complementary features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple addition of acoustic information can treat modalities as noise; including a filtering mechanism improved final F1 to 71.1% (sarcasm) and 82.0% (humor) in the proposed model — ~4% and ~2% gains compared to the model without filtering. Design fusion to filter noisy modality signals and amplify complementary cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-learning vs separate learning trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-learning of sarcasm and humor (shared base architecture with task-specific output branches) can reduce parameter count and complexity but may slightly lower classification performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint model yielded F1-scores of 68.6% and 81.4% (sarcasm, humor) vs separate-learning slightly higher; joint learning required ~50% fewer parameters. Consider joint learning when parameter/complexity reduction is important, but validate performance drop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context window choice for baseline/contextual comparative systems
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating or adapting existing contextual systems (MUStARD, Ghosh et al.), define a consistent context window (authors used previous five utterances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a pre-defined context (e.g., previous five utterances) to ensure fair comparative evaluation and to match the contextual modeling assumptions of baseline systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of code-mixing (English word fraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model performance correlates with the level of English words in code-mixed utterances: more English words generally improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors sampled two test sets (∼18 English words/utterance vs ∼1 English word/utterance) and observed markedly better precision/recall/F1 for the high-English set. Account for code-mixing distribution in dataset design and evaluation; consider multilingual embeddings for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention interpretability and heatmap analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze attention heatmaps (textual, acoustic, cross-modal) to interpret which contextual utterances and modalities the model attends to for each target utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High attention weights should correlate with contextual/multimodal semantics (examples in Figures 3 and 4 show such correlation); use heatmaps for qualitative error analysis and to justify model decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset and annotation standards (MaSaC)
rubrics_metrics.description: MaSaC is a qualitative multi-modal dataset for sarcasm detection and humor classification in Hindi-English code-mixed conversational dialogs: >15,000 utterances across 1,190 dialogs from an Indian television comedy show, collected, cleaned, and annotated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or using such datasets, ensure cleaning and annotation quality, document modality quality (e.g., low-quality video frames affect visual feature usefulness), and provide dataset splits and benchmarks for reproducibility.
